questions.q: A T-SQL developer writes SELECT * FROM Opportunity in SOQL and it fails. Why?
options: Opportunity is not a real Salesforce object
SOQL has no SELECT * — every field must be named explicitly, a deliberate constraint tied to API cost and governor limits
SELECT * works fine in SOQL; the error must be unrelated
SOQL doesn't support the FROM clause
questions.explain: SOQL requires every field to be explicitly named — there is no wildcard SELECT * as in T-SQL.

questions.q: What does SOQL call what SQL calls a 'table'?
options: A schema
A record
A field
An object
questions.explain: SOQL terminology: object = table, field = column, record = row.

questions.q: Why is it good practice to include Id in almost every SOQL query, per this lesson?
options: Id is the record's real, unique identifier, useful for looking up or linking back to that exact record later
Id is required to sort query results
SOQL queries fail without Id in the SELECT list
Id determines which fields are visible due to field-level security
questions.explain: Including Id is a habit worth building even when not strictly needed for the report, since it's the record's real unique identifier.

questions.q: How do comparison and logical operators like =, !=, >, AND, and OR behave in SOQL WHERE clauses compared to T-SQL?
options: SOQL has no comparison operators at all
Logical operators like AND/OR are not supported in SOQL
SOQL only supports the equals operator
They work exactly the same way as in T-SQL
questions.explain: Comparison and logical operators in SOQL WHERE clauses work exactly like their T-SQL counterparts.

questions.q: Why does knowing your org's actual field values (like StageName's real values) matter for writing a correct WHERE clause, per this lesson?
options: Field values are standardized identically across every Salesforce org with no customization possible
StageName is not a real, queryable field
WHERE clauses in SOQL don't actually filter on field values
Every org customizes its own picklist values (e.g. sales stage names), so filtering on the wrong assumed value silently returns no or wrong results
questions.explain: This ties directly back to Salesforce Fundamentals' data-model teaching — org-specific field values must be known, not assumed.
